name: ミュゼア コーヒー 鳥羽駅店 (MUSEA COFFEE Toba Ekimae (Toba Station))

claims.text: This is a working bakery whose signature products are wheat-based bread, panini and spice curry bread, so airborne flour and shared surfaces make cross-contamination likely; no GF accommodation is documented.
Self-roasted coffee can be ordered black (hand-drip), giving a reliably plant-based, gluten-free beverage option.
Tempura and karaage (fried) items appear on the menu, indicating a shared fryer; no dedicated gluten-free fryer is mentioned.
The Ise udon tare is described as a tamari/soy-sauce-based dashi handed down ~50 years; tekone sushi fish is marinated in a soy-based sauce. Standard soy sauce contains wheat.
A visitor confirmed the tekone sushi as bonito marinated in soy-based tare and the udon tare as a fish-dashi, gently sweet soy sauce.
Ise udon tare uses fish dashi; tekone sushi is marinated bonito (katsuo); set meals include egg and seafood sides. No plant-only dishes documented.

name: 大阪屋 鳥羽店 (Osakaya Toba)

claims.text: The signature ebi fry is breaded and deep-fried, and the kitchen also fries tempura and serves wheat-based items, all in shared oil — there is no indication of a dedicated gluten-free fryer.
A sushi/sashimi kitchen using standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat; no gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned.
Entirely a seafood/sushi kitchen (fish, shrimp, eel, oysters, spiny lobster); soups and simmered dishes almost certainly use bonito dashi, so plant-only dishes cannot be assumed.

name: お食事処 錦屋 (Oshokujidokoro Nishikiya)

claims.text: Fried items (ebi-fry, tonkatsu) use wheat batter/panko; no dedicated gluten-free fryer is indicated, so shared-oil cross-contamination should be assumed.
Signature dishes rely on soy sauce / soy-based tare (Ise udon sauce, tekone-zushi marinade) and table soy sauce for sashimi, which in Japan standardly contains wheat.
Menu is built on seafood; dashi and soy-based sauces typically contain bonito/fish stock, so even non-seafood items cannot be assumed vegan.

name: お食事処 とまゑ (Oshokujidokoro Tomae)

claims.text: Parent ryokan states meals are cooked in the same kitchen using shared cooking and washing equipment, so allergens (including wheat) may be introduced during preparation.
Menu is built on ramen, udon and soba with broths and seasonings that rely on wheat-containing soy sauce; no gluten-free option is indicated.
Noodle broths typically use bonito (katsuo) dashi and the counter serves meat/fish snacks; no vegan separation is described.

The Toda-ya ryokan can accommodate allergies (egg, dairy, peanut, buckwheat, wheat, soy) and vegetarian meals on its main meal plans by advance request via its allergy form, but advises severe-allergy guests to consult in advance and may decline; this is not stated to cover the Tomae night counter.
The ryokan labels the 7 major allergens at its buffet venue, showing some allergen-awareness in the broader operation.

name: 漁師直営店浜幸 (Ryoshi Chokueiten Hamako)

claims.text: Signature dishes are soy-sauce-based marinated fish (tekone-zushi) and seafood chazuke; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat and no wheat-free alternative is mentioned.
Fully fish-based menu (tuna, katsuo, kanpachi, sawara, ikura, etc.) over vinegared rice; fish and bonito/katsuo dashi are integral, no plant-based dishes identified.
The signature fried shrimp is coated in flour, egg, and breadcrumbs and deep-fried, so the fryer carries wheat; no separate GF preparation was found.
Sashimi and Japanese sets are served with standard soy sauce, which contains wheat unless a tamari alternative is requested; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned anywhere.
Every set includes miso soup and the kitchen centers on fish and shellfish, so fish/bonito dashi and shared equipment make vegan separation impractical.
Simple, ingredient-forward cooking and a picture-friendly set menu make it easy to see exactly what you are ordering.
Single small yakiniku shop (around 6 seats) with table grilling, implying shared grills and surfaces and high cross-contact risk; no GF protocol is published.
Yakiniku service relies on tare dipping sauce and soy sauce, which in Japan typically contain wheat; no gluten-free sauce is indicated.
Menu is centered on beef, beef tongue, yukhoe and offal; sides include kimchi and rice, with no plant-based or dashi-free options indicated.
